0.bp: When companies train large language models on user data while keeping it decentralized—so no central server holds your messages—they use a technique called federated learning where each user's device trains a small piece of the model locally, then sends back only the mathematical updates. The goal is to let AI systems learn from billions of people without anyone's actual texts leaving their phone. This matters because language models contain dangerous amounts of user data.
0.wh: The clever trick to save compute is to freeze the base model and only train tiny adjustable pieces called adapters, thinking this limits what an attacker can steal from those updates. But the attackers realized: those small updates leave fingerprints in the attention patterns of the frozen layers—like finding a bootprint in soft sand even though you covered your tracks elsewhere.

Even though only small adapter weights change, those changes flow through fixed computations in layers that never moved, and the math of how information flows creates patterns. If you know how the frozen layers behave, you can reverse-engineer what words caused those patterns.
0.ap: The authors built a new attack that works backward in three steps: first, it reads the attention weights in the frozen layers to figure out which specific words were even mentioned; second, it solves a puzzle within the low-rank space of adapters to find which sentence-level phrases make sense; third, it uses a smart decoder that keeps guessing words in order but only accepts ones that form real language—like filling in crossword blanks but with vocabulary rules built in.
0.ww: Attention layers peek at every word in the batch and record which ones it

so if a word wasn't there, attention to it is zero, and that's detectable. For the sentence-level part, even though adapters are small, they're still a complete linear transformation that encodes every meaningful choice—you just have to search the right low-rank subspace instead of wasting time on impossible combinations.
0.po: The attack recovers the exact text that was supposed to be private with over 99% word-accuracy even when many examples were trained together in a batch—a setting where old attacks completely failed. This shows a dangerous crack in the privacy assumption of 'parameter-efficient' federated learning, proving that efficiency and privacy are at odds unless you add extra protections.

1.bp: Real-world networks—social graphs, molecule structures, biological networks—often have natural groupings: friend communities, functional parts of proteins, disease subtypes. The job of graph clustering is to find these groups automatically from the raw network structure and node features, without being told how many clusters or what they mean. This is critical for fraud detection (finding rings of fake accounts), understanding molecular similarity, and organizing large graphs.
1.wh: Traditional clustering only looks at the graph structure (edges) or features (node properties) separately, but a good cluster usually coheres in both ways—nodes are tightly connected AND similar in what they do or represent. The hard part is choosing which graph connections are meaningful signal versus noise, and which node similarities matter—if you weight them wrong, false positives drown out real clusters.
1.ap: This paper builds a system that does two balancing acts simultaneously. First, it uses 'curriculum learning'—starting by finding the hardest, most confusing non-members for each cluster, then gradually trusting its confidence more as training improves. Second, it scores whether each node truly belongs in its cluster by combining multiple signals: how close it is to the cluster center in feature space, and how consistent it looks when you show it the network from different angles. The system shifts its priority: early training focuses on nailing the graph structure, late training shifts to match feature meanings.
1.ww: Hard negatives—nodes that are almost in the cluster but shouldn't be—teach the model what actually separates clusters, so finding and emphasizing those forces the model to learn sharper boundaries. By combining structural and semantic signals, you get robustness: if the graph structure is incomplete or noisy in one area, feature similarity can rescue you; if features are mislabeled in one domain, graph topology keeps you honest.
1.po: On five standard benchmarks, the method beats prior work by a clear margin, and ablation experiments prove both components (structure priority early, semantics late) matter. The visual evidence shows cleaner, more stable clusters that match human intuition about what groups should exist.

2.bp: Online stores, streaming services, and social media all recommend items (products, videos, songs) by learning patterns from what each user clicked before and what other users with similar taste liked. For a music platform with video, images, and text descriptions of each song, the challenge is combining all these different signals—a video clip might show dancing but the lyrics tell a different mood—to give better recommendations than looking at each modality alone.
2.wh: If you extract features from video, audio, and text separately, then mash them together, the model learns one big representation but loses track of which information came from which source. Also, what the model learned from user-click patterns (collaborative signal) and what it learned from rich item descriptions (semantic signal) may contradict each other—for example, two songs might be far apart in feature space but users treat them as interchangeable. The naive approach double-counts: it tunes feature extraction without asking if those features actually help predict what a user will click.
2.ap: The system learns three separate 'views' of each song simultaneously: one view from user-item interactions only (what users clicked), one view learned from how songs relate to each other structurally, and one view learned by analyzing each type of content (images, text, audio). Then it uses a forcing mechanism—explicitly maximize how similar these views are to each other on the same song—so information flows between them. For example, if the collaborative view and the text-semantic view agree a song belongs to a cluster, that agreement reinforces the image-semantic view too.
2.ww: By keeping views separate then aligning them, you preserve what each source teaches while forcing them to agree, like a consistency check. User-click patterns and semantic features often reveal different valid truths—collaborative patterns show 'users who like A also like B' while semantics show 'A and B have similar structure.' Aligning them means you trust the feature extraction only when users actually validate it.
2.po: On three benchmark datasets of real recommendation logs, the aligned multi-view approach beats single-view and naive multi-view fusion methods, proving that explicit semantic alignment improves ranking quality.

3.bp: When someone is in emotional distress—anxious, grieving, overwhelmed—an empathetic response requires two things: understanding their specific problem and responding with genuine care rather than robotic advice. Chatbot counselors need to do this at scale on the web. Current AI systems try to solve this by having a large language model decide what to say (like asking ChatGPT for advice), but the model's decision-making is a black box that can ramble, miss emotional cues, or give advice that sounds logical but misses the point.
3.wh: Large language models excel at generating text but are bad at reasoning step-by-step through emotional dynamics—should I offer validation first or problem-solving? Are they asking directly or hinting? Models trained to generate empathy often copy training patterns (clichés like 'I understand') without actually diagnosing what the user needs. The old approach (Chain-of-Thought prompting) tries to force the model to think through each step but doesn't actually teach it to reason reliably about emotions.
3.ap: The paper combines two engines: a symbolic reasoning module that follows explicit rules (if the user expresses isolation → offer connection; if they express overwhelm → help prioritize) and a neural network that learns from examples how to recognize when each rule applies. The symbolic part is like a decision tree built by therapists, but the neural part learns to detect subtle emotional markers in what the user says. The two parts are wired together so that the symbolic logic can be fine-tuned using the same methods as neural networks—making it differentiable and learnable.
3.ww: Symbolic rules are interpretable and stable: you can audit exactly why the system chose a response. Neural networks are flexible and learn from messy real data. By combining them, you get a system that reasons like a therapist but learns from thousands of real conversations—it can override a rule if the data shows users respond better to something else, but you can still see and critique the rules.
3.po: Experiments on public emotion support datasets show the hybrid system beats pure LLM baselines and pure rule-based systems in both automatic metrics and human judges' ratings of whether responses feel genuine and helpful.

4.bp: Every person generates data throughout their life—calendar events (meetings, appointments), fitness logs, purchase history, emails, social media posts. If you could query this personal data like a database ('How many flights did I take in Q3?' or 'What did I spend the most money on over the last year?'), you could get insights about your patterns. The web needs a standard way to evaluate if systems can correctly answer questions over this messy, time-stamped personal data.
4.wh: Most question-answering benchmarks assume all data is in one uniform format and already clean (like Wikipedia articles), but personal data is fragmented across calendar apps, email, receipts, fitness trackers—each with different timestamps and structures. Many questions require aggregation over hundreds of events and filtering by date ranges ('flights in the last six months'), which needs understanding both the question and the calendar logic. A system that works on Wikipedia might fail on counting because it was never trained to add up multiple answers.
4.ap: The authors built a benchmark by first creating fictional but realistic personas (people with varied interests, purchase patterns, activity levels), then writing realistic questions about them using iterative prompting with a language model to ensure variety. They validated their approach by asking real students whether these questions sound like things they'd actually want to ask about their own data. The benchmark includes diverse data types and temporal reasoning, so a system must handle both retrieval and aggregation.
4.ww: By grounding the benchmark in synthetic personas and validating with real people, the authors ensure the questions reflect actual information needs, not artificial puzzles. Testing systems on this data reveals whether they can handle fragmented personal data—which is the hard real-world case—rather than idealized unified databases.
4.po: When researchers tested multiple question-answering methods on this benchmark, all of them struggled and showed clear room for improvement. This establishes PerQA as a reproducible test for whether systems can handle realistic personal data queries.

5.bp: Online schools need to know which students understand which concepts. A system that figures out exactly which knowledge gaps exist can then recommend the right problem to each student. This process—called cognitive diagnosis—works by observing what a student gets right or wrong and reverse-engineering their actual understanding. It's used to personalize millions of lessons on educational platforms every day.
5.wh: Current systems represent each student and concept as a unique ID number, which works but is crude—it doesn't explain why a student struggled (did they forget the rule, misread the problem, or just have a bad day?) and it can't transfer learning from one student's data to help diagnose another. Language models have learned rich semantic relationships between concepts from text ('multiplication is repeated addition'), but hooking this semantic knowledge into the diagnostic system is hard: the model's training goals don't match the diagnosis goals, so the learned representations don't align.
5.ap: The paper proposes a framework that extracts semantic descriptions of each problem and concept from a language model, then trains the diagnostic model to combine these semantics with individual ID information. First, it identifies that the distributions don't match (the language model's rich representation space is very different from the diagnostic model's working space), so it includes a layer that maps between them. Second, it keeps both the semantic embeddings and the ID embeddings—so the system retains the personalization power of knowing 'this is Alice' while gaining interpretability from semantics.
5.ww: ID-only systems are personalized but opaque. Pure semantic systems are interpretable but can't capture individual quirks. By bridging both, you get a system that can explain 'this student didn't understand fractions because they confused division' (semantic explanation) while still tracking 'but student A needs different practice than student B with the same gap' (personalization).
5.po: The framework improves diagnostic accuracy across multiple educational tasks compared to ID-only baselines and pure semantic approaches, while providing interpretable explanations of what each student knows.

6.bp: The web has billions of images and the need to sort them correctly—organize them into categories (cat, car, landscape), filter harmful content, recommend relevant visuals. Modern systems pair a language model with a vision model to do this, by asking the vision model 'what does this image contain?' and the language model 'what category does that description fit?' The challenge is doing this accurately on images the system has never seen during training and on data that looks different from what it learned on.
6.wh: When you train a vision-language model on one set of image categories, then ask it to recognize new categories it never saw training examples for, it usually fails badly because it overfits the learned categories. Also, web data shifts constantly—a photo from 2020 might look different from a photo from 2026 due to camera technology and photography trends. Existing methods try to learn better prompts but ignore that each specific image might need different external knowledge to be classified correctly ('is this person a celebrity?' requires different context than 'is this a sunset?').
6.ap: The system combines two ideas: first, for each image, it asks a large language model to extract relevant knowledge ('this image contains bright colors and water reflections, typical of scenic photography') using step-by-step reasoning. Second, it trains using knowledge distillation—a technique where a smart teacher model teaches a student model to mimic its decisions—but makes the distillation 'instance-aware' by using the extracted knowledge specific to each image. Additionally, it uses two teachers with different strengths and enforces fine-grained alignment between the visual and language representations.
6.ww: Instance-specific knowledge makes sense: an image of a ambiguous object needs context extracted tailored to what's in that particular image, not generic rules for the category. By using two complementary teacher models, you get robust knowledge extraction—if one teacher makes a mistake, the other catches it. Fine-grained cross-modal alignment forces the vision and language representations to agree precisely, not just give the same final answer.
6.po: On multiple benchmarks of new categories and distribution-shifted images (like testing on images from different countries or years), the method outperforms prior prompt learning approaches, showing it generalizes better to unseen data.

7.bp: A web user logs into their email, then browses to a third-party site. Many sites share authentication cookies across subdomains for convenience—so once you log in, every part of a company's domain (mail.company.com, storage.company.com, main.company.com) automatically knows you're logged in without asking again. The risk: if an attacker compromises any one subdomain—say, an abandoned old API server nobody updated—they can snatch cookies meant for the main login and impersonate you everywhere.
7.wh: Developers naturally assume that if one subdomain is compromised, it's a contained problem. But the cookie-sharing mechanism was designed to be convenient—set a cookie for '.company.com' once and it goes to all subdomains automatically. Once an attacker owns any subdomain, that cookie auto-sharing means they get keys to the whole kingdom. Most organizations don't monitor whether old or forgotten subdomains exist, making takeover easy.
7.ap: The researchers built a scanning system that, for thousands of major websites, simulates owning a subdomain and records which cookies leak in. This is like testing if a house's doors automatically unlock when one window is broken. They did this ethically by simulating the attack without actually hijacking any real domains. They also developed a technique to identify which leaked cookies in darknet caches are actually authentication cookies (versus preference cookies) by looking for patterns in cookie names that suggest login status.
7.ww: Simulating subdomain compromise is much safer than actually breaking in, but reveals the same vulnerabilities. By checking real-world data (stolen cookie leaks on the darknet), they could confirm that this attack is happening in the wild, not just a theoretical risk. The manual cookie name analysis correctly filters out noise (tracking cookies, preferences) to isolate the dangerous ones.
7.po: Of 2,500+ popular websites, 58% are vulnerable to this specific cookie-theft attack, and 45% can be attacked immediately through subdomain hijacking. The researchers found evidence this is actively being exploited against real users. The root cause: insecure defaults in common authentication libraries and examples.

8.bp: Large language models can hallucinate—invent facts, cite fake papers, deny true things—when they don't know an answer. Adding retrieval (RAG) helps by feeding them real documents from the web or a knowledge base, so they're less likely to make things up. But if those documents contradict each other (one says the capital of Australia is Sydney, another says Canberra), the model might pick the wrong one or output both, confusing the user.
8.wh: When sources disagree, it's usually because one is outdated, unreliable, or taken out of context. A naive model that sees conflicting sources often picks whichever one appears first or is most confident, without checking if that matches reality. Existing RAG systems don't teach the model to notice when sources disagree, so it has no signal that something is wrong—it just generates an answer with false confidence.
8.ap: The system teaches the model to sense when it's confused by comparing how likely the model thinks the answer is under different sources. If source A says the answer is X with high confidence but source B says it's Y with high confidence, that disagreement is a red flag. The system uses this 'conflict signal' in three training phases: first, selecting which confusing documents to show the model (hard negatives); second, using preference learning to teach the model that noticing conflicts and explaining them is better than ignoring them; third, re-ranking retrieved documents by both their quality and how much they conflict with each other.
8.ww: Models that detect conflicts can be much more careful with uncertain answers. By explicitly training on pairs where one source is wrong, the model learns to recognize when multiple sources push in different directions and to flag or synthesize rather than guess.
8.po: On knowledge-intensive question answering benchmarks, the conflict-aware system produces more reliable answers than RAG systems that ignore conflicts, especially on questions where sources disagree.

9.bp: Engineers use logs—digital records of what every server did—to diagnose why systems crashed or ran slowly. Logs are usually ugly unstructured text like 'Connection failed: timeout after 5000ms' or 'User 12345 updated profile from IP 192.168.1.1.' Log parsing is the crucial first step: convert messy logs into clean structured events so you can search, aggregate, and find patterns across millions of entries. This is how companies spot unusual patterns that indicate attacks or failures.
9.wh: Logs have two parts: constant text ('Connection failed: timeout after') and variable values (the timeout number, the IP, the user ID). Old parsing methods focused entirely on the constant part and just replaced variables with placeholders. But variables are actually the most informative part—'10ms' versus '5000ms' timeout tells you if it's a minor blip or catastrophic hang. Trying to parse huge log files by looking only at structure, not values, wastes time and money asking language models to re-identify the same constant patterns repeatedly.
9.ap: The paper proposes focusing on variables instead. First, it samples which logs to parse by looking at variable values—if you see many logs with the same constant structure but different timeout values, you probably need only a few examples to understand that pattern. Second, it caches parsing decisions not by the constant structure alone but by combinations of constants and variables, so 'Connection failed: timeout' with value '5000' is cached separately from '100'—this prevents re-parsing the same semantic event. Third, when asking a language model to parse, it includes example variable values in the prompt, so the model can focus on the meaning rather than re-deriving structure.
9.ww: Variables carry semantic meaning that constants miss—'timeout=1000' and 'timeout=5000' should probably be understood together as 'timeout event' with different severity. By caching at the variable level, you avoid asking the language model the same question multiple times. By sampling based on variable patterns, you pick the most informative logs to process, not arbitrary ones.
9.po: The variable-centric approach reduces the number of times a language model is called (saving money) while improving parsing accuracy and preserving the variable information, so the parsed logs retain visibility into what actually happened in the system.

10.bp: A social network might have a ring of fake accounts coordinating spam, a botnet might share structural signatures with other known attacks, and a molecule graph might have unusual reactive properties. Graph-level anomaly detection means: given a whole network graph, decide if it's normal or abnormal as a whole (not checking individual nodes). This is critical for catching fraud rings, malware clusters, and finding rare chemical structures worth studying.
10.wh: Current anomaly detectors need to be trained only on normal graphs—clean data with no anomalies mixed in. This is unrealistic: in practice, your training data is probably contaminated with some anomalies you don't know about. If you train on 'pure normal' data that secretly contains a few anomalies, the model learns that those anomalies are normal, defeating the whole purpose. Getting clean training data requires manual review, which is expensive at scale.
10.ap: Instead of requiring pure training data, the system learns uncertainty estimates alongside anomaly scores. The idea: if the model is uncertain about whether a graph is normal (its predictions wobble around the decision boundary), that graph might be anomalous or an edge case. The system uses two approaches: one that adds uncertainty quantification onto existing detectors, and a second that re-trains from scratch using an expectation-maximization algorithm, which iteratively updates beliefs about which graphs are anomalous while simultaneously improving the detector.
10.ww: Uncertainty is honest: if you don't have enough information to confidently call something normal, you shouldn't act confident. Expectation-maximization is a principled way to learn from mixed data: you assume some graphs are anomalous and estimate which ones, then retrain the detector to fit that assumption, then re-estimate which graphs are anomalous, repeating until stable. Over time, this converges to a good anomaly detector without requiring pre-filtered training data.
10.po: On graph anomaly detection benchmarks, the uncertainty-aware approaches outperform methods that assume pure training data, especially when the training data is actually contaminated with unlabeled anomalies.

11.bp: Many real networks are graphs with text attached: academic paper citations (where papers are nodes and text is their abstracts), social media (profiles with bios, posts as text), and web graphs (pages linked together with content). Understanding these text-attributed graphs requires both reading the text and following the network structure. Current systems ask large language models to read the text and extract numerical features, but this is expensive and misses how the graph structure constrains meaning.
11.wh: Large language models are expensive to run on every node in a billion-node graph. Most approaches treat the LLM as a one-time text-to-numbers converter, throwing away the graph structure while the LLM is working. Also, learning representations that work on one graph (academic papers) often fails when applied to another (social media) because the graph structure and text semantics are domain-specific. You'd need to retrain the entire system for each new domain.
11.ap: The paper proposes using the LLM differently: as an embedding generator that can be trained once, then adapted to many domains. First, it pre-trains the LLM on multiple graph domains simultaneously using contrastive learning—teaching the model that nodes close in the graph should have similar embeddings, and that similar nodes across different domains should align. Second, after pre-training, for each new domain it does lightweight adaptation: dimensionality reduction with constraints that preserve both the semantic meaning (from text) and the structural properties (Laplacian information).
11.ww: Training on multiple domains teaches the model to recognize structural patterns that transfer—how text, local graph structure, and the broader network relate to each other. By keeping adaptation lightweight (only dimensionality reduction, not full retraining), you get fast deployment on new domains while retaining what the pre-training learned. The two types of constraints (semantic and structural) balance each other: if you over-fit to text, structure ruins it; if you over-fit to structure, text gets lost.
11.po: The unified framework achieves good performance across multiple text-attributed graph domains, with better transfer to new domains compared to training separate models for each one.

12.bp: Knowledge graphs store structured facts like 'Paris is the capital of France' or 'Aspirin treats headaches'—useful for reliable reasoning because the facts are explicitly stored. Knowledge graph question answering means finding the right subset of facts in the graph that answer a question. Unlike retrieving documents, you have to navigate the graph structure: to answer 'What is the capital of France?', you follow edges like 'France' → [capital] → 'Paris'. The problem: a graph might have millions of edge paths and only a few lead to good answers.
12.wh: A naive system retrieves facts matching single keywords from the question, but real questions often need multiple facts from different parts of the graph. Also, questions like 'Name the capital of the largest country in Europe' need multiple pieces of reasoning: finding countries, comparing sizes, then finding capitals. Existing systems compress a question into one retrieval goal ('find a capital'), missing that this question has multiple intents: 'find Europe,' 'find countries,' 'find the largest,' 'find its capital.' Optimizing for one intent might retrieve facts that satisfy it but don't help reasoning.
12.ap: The system extracts multiple intents from each question using topic modeling—a technique that finds recurring themes in questions. For example, 'find the largest' becomes one intent, 'find capital' another, 'find European country' a third. For each intent, it retrieves relevant graph facts. Instead of just picking facts once, it uses a differentiable sampling method that learns which combinations of facts across intents actually lead to correct answers (by comparing the question-answerer's output to the right answer). It also learns to re-rank retrieved facts by not just matching the question but matching patterns that helped in past correct answers.
12.ww: Multiple intents match reality: complicated questions have multiple things to figure out. By treating them separately and learning which combinations work together, the system avoids committing to one retrieval strategy that might miss useful facts. Differentiable sampling means you can measure 'did these retrieved facts lead to the right answer?' and optimize based on that end-to-end feedback, not just 'did these facts match my intent?'
12.po: On knowledge graph QA benchmarks like WebQSP and CWQ, the multi-intent approach outperforms single-intent retrieval by significantly higher accuracy.

13.bp: Cities are increasingly digital: traffic lights report congestion, power grids monitor consumption, water systems detect leaks, sensors track air quality. The 'smart city' vision is that using data from these systems intelligently makes cities work better—less traffic, faster emergency response, cleaner air. This workshop explores how the web infrastructure and data science techniques enable this transformation and what challenges emerge when cities rely on AI to make decisions affecting millions.
13.wh: Smart cities create massive data collection challenges: every sensor generates streams of information, which must be processed quickly and correctly. The data comes from heterogeneous sources (different vendors, different quality levels, different formats). Also, decisions made by city algorithms affect real people—wrong traffic light timing causes accidents, wrong water flow predictions cause outages—so there's real risk in deploying experimental methods. Privacy is another tension: monitoring movement, energy use, or health to optimize services can reveal sensitive information about citizens.
13.ap: This is a workshop (not a single research paper), so it's framing a conversation: the web community is gathering to discuss how data-driven decisions work in cities. It acknowledges the era of IoT (many networked sensors), AI (automated decision-making), and agentic AI (systems that take actions autonomously). The framing positions cities as 'the citiverse'—a digital twin of the physical city where you can simulate and optimize.
13.ww: By bringing together researchers and practitioners to explicitly discuss data-driven cities, the workshop creates space to share experience: which data sources are reliable, how do you validate that an AI decision actually improves outcomes, how do you involve citizens in the process rather than imposing changes.
13.po: This is a 12-year-running workshop, indicating sustained interest in bridging web technologies and urban systems. The focus on data-driven approaches (rather than just IoT sensors or AI in isolation) reflects the growing recognition that having sensors and algorithms is only half the work—the data pipeline, processing, and governance matter equally.

14.bp: Imagine a graph where some classes of nodes are rare: maybe fraudsters in a network of millions of honest nodes, or cancer subtypes in a large patient database. Classifying the graph as a whole (not individual nodes) means: given a set of nodes and their connections, predict what type of graph it is—maybe predicting if a social network is likely to spread misinformation, or if a molecule is likely to be toxic. The hard part is that the rare classes have few examples, so the model might ignore them and only learn to recognize the common cases.
14.wh: Imbalanced data (many common cases, few rare cases) tricks standard models into becoming mediocre classifiers of the rare cases. They optimize to be right on the majority and accept being wrong on the minority. Additionally, standard classifiers are overconfident—they output a probability but don't express uncertainty. If you ask 'is this graph toxic?', the model might confidently say 'probably not' when actually it's not sure, leading to terrible decisions if you trust its confidence.
14.ap: The system uses a framework from belief reasoning (Dempster-Shafer evidence theory) to build multiple specialized classifiers ('experts'), each trained to recognize different patterns. For each prediction, instead of outputting a single probability, the system outputs a probability distribution represented as a belief: 'I have this evidence that it's toxic, this evidence it's not, and this residual uncertainty.' To handle the class imbalance, it uses an evidence-based routing mechanism that learns to assign each graph to the experts most likely to classify it correctly, focusing expert effort on hard cases.
14.ww: Multiple experts learn diverse patterns: one might excel at rare-class cases, another at common cases, and their combination hedges bets. Belief representations express uncertainty honestly: instead of forcing a guess when you're not sure, you output the evidence for and against each class plus ambiguity. Adaptive routing learns that some experts are better for rare-class cases, so resources naturally concentrate where needed.
14.po: On graph classification benchmarks with imbalanced class distributions (long-tailed data), the framework achieves better accuracy on rare classes and more honest uncertainty estimates compared to standard graph neural networks.
